title: America's Landscapes
description: Ten informative texts on the landscapes of the United States: how the Grand Canyon formed, the Everglades, the grasses of the Great Plains, Yellowstone's geysers and history, the redwood forests, the Mississippi delta, the Alaskan tundra, the Sonoran Desert and a ranger's view of the canyon.
topic: Geography and natural history of the United States

lessons.title: How the Grand Canyon Formed
lessons.summary: An explanation of how a river, rising land, rain and ice made the Grand Canyon.
lessons.text:
Standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon, most visitors ask the same question: how could a river make a hole this big? The canyon is about 277 miles long, up to 18 miles wide and more than a mile deep. From the top, the Colorado River looks like a thin green thread. And yet this river, helped by rain, ice and a great deal of time, is the main reason the canyon exists.

To understand the process, it helps to look at a diagram. Scientists usually draw the canyon wall as a simple diagram of flat layers of rock, one on top of the other, like the layers of a cake. Most of the layers were laid down in very different worlds: in shallow seas, along beaches or in deserts of sand. The oldest rocks, at the bottom, are close to 2 billion years old; the youngest, at the top, are about 270 million.

First, the land rose. Over millions of years, forces deep in the earth slowly pushed this whole region up by thousands of feet. The river kept its path and went on cutting down into the rising rock, like a knife held firmly in place while a cake is pushed up against it. Most of this cutting probably happened in the last 5 or 6 million years.

Second, the canyon grew wider. Water gets into cracks, freezes, expands and breaks the rock apart, and summer storms wash stones and mud into the river, which carries them away.

This explains the canyon's distinctive shape. Its walls look like a giant set of stairs, with steep cliffs and gentle slopes, and that is no coincidence. Hard layers of rock stand firmly and form cliffs. Soft layers wear away quickly and form slopes. When a soft layer wears away beneath a hard one, it begins to undermine it. Once it is undermined from below, the hard rock breaks off and falls. In this way the cliffs move back, and the canyon has grown considerably wider. Every side canyon shows the same distinctive steps.

The proof of this story is evident to anyone who looks carefully. Across the canyon, the same layers appear on the opposite wall, at the same height and in the same order. The similarity is evident even without special training, and it is no coincidence either: it tells us that the two walls were once one piece of land, later cut in two.

Scientists can date the rocks accurately, but dating the cutting itself accurately is considerably harder. What has not changed is human curiosity. In 1869, curiosity led John Wesley Powell to take a small group of men down the river in wooden boats. Today, the same curiosity brings millions of visitors to the canyon every year.

Questions:
What is the main reason the Grand Canyon exists?
The Colorado River, helped by rain, ice and time, is the main reason.
How do scientists usually draw the canyon wall?
They draw it as a simple diagram of flat layers of rock, one on top of the other.
Why do the walls look like a set of stairs?
Hard layers form cliffs and soft layers form slopes, and a soft layer can undermine the hard rock above it until it breaks off.
What does the similarity between the two walls tell us?
It tells us that the two walls were once one piece of land.
What led John Wesley Powell down the river in 1869?
Curiosity led him down the river.

lessons.title: A River of Grass
lessons.summary: How water once moved through the Everglades, how people changed it, and why repairing it is hard.
lessons.text:
Most people imagine the Everglades as a dark swamp of trees and still water. In fact, most of it is a wide, open plain of grass, and its water is not still at all. Before people changed it, water from rain and from Lake Okeechobee spread across southern Florida in a shallow sheet up to 60 miles wide. Often only a few inches deep, it moved south toward the sea at about 100 feet a day. That is why the writer Marjory Stoneman Douglas, in a famous book from 1947, called the Everglades a river of grass.

In the wet summer, much of the land is underwater, and in very wet years almost all of it is underwater. In the dry winter, the water slowly falls, and fish crowd into the pools that remain. For birds that wade through shallow water to hunt, this is the season of plenty. Ecologists use the word guild for a group of species that live from the same resource in a similar way, and these wading birds form a guild that depends on falling water. When the water falls at the right speed, they nest by the thousands. When it falls too fast, or rises again at the wrong time, the fish spread out, and the birds depart without raising their young.

The Everglades has a human history, too. Between 1817 and 1858, during three wars with the United States Army, many Seminole people retreated deep into the Everglades. For them, this wet country was a kind of asylum, a place where soldiers could rarely follow. Many of their families still live in South Florida today.

In the last century, the main human interference was drainage. Engineers dug canals and built walls of earth to dry the land for farms and towns. Roads added a further kind of interference. An old road across the south of Florida, and later an interstate highway to its north, worked like low dams, blocking the water's slow journey south.

The results were both direct and indirect. The direct result was that much of the Everglades became drier and smaller. The indirect results took longer to see. Dry ground burned more often. Salt water from the sea moved into places that had been fresh. The wading birds declined sharply.

Since 2000, the state and the federal government have worked on a long rehabilitation of the Everglades. Parts of the old road have been lifted onto bridges so that water can pass beneath them, and the interstate has openings that let water and animals move underneath. These are not cosmetic changes. A cosmetic change would only improve the view; these changes let the water flow again. Still, rehabilitation is tricky. Millions of people in South Florida need the same water for drinking, and they also need protection from floods. It is slow and expensive work, but most experts agree that it is worth doing.

Questions:
Why did Marjory Stoneman Douglas call the Everglades a river of grass?
A shallow sheet of water moved slowly south across a wide plain of grass.
Why do the wading birds sometimes depart without raising their young?
They depart when the water falls too fast or rises again at the wrong time.
Why was the Everglades a kind of asylum for the Seminole people?
It was a place where soldiers could rarely follow them.
Why is the rehabilitation of the Everglades tricky?
Millions of people need the same water and also need protection from floods.

lessons.title: The Grasses of the Great Plains
lessons.summary: How rain, roots, fire and buffalo shaped the grass of the Great Plains, and what the Dust Bowl taught.
lessons.text:
If you drive west across the middle of the United States, the land grows flatter, wider and emptier. These are the Great Plains, a huge region of grass that stretches from Texas to Canada, and from the Rocky Mountains east to roughly the Missouri River. To a scientist, the grass forms several different worlds, and the main thing that separates them is rain.

Rain on the plains follows a clear pattern of inequality. Air from the west loses most of its moisture over the mountains, so the western plains are dry. Air from the Gulf of Mexico brings more rain to the east. As a result, the eastern plains may receive twice as much rain in a year as the western plains, and this inequality of rain explains the inequality of the grass.

In the wetter east grew the tallgrass prairie. By late summer, its grasses reached a person's thigh, then a person's elbow, and in good years some stood taller than a man on a horse. Farther west, the grass grew to about knee or thigh height. In the driest west, the shortgrass grew only a few inches high, low enough for a crow walking through it to see over the top.

What we see is only part of the story. Most of a prairie grass plant lives underground, in roots that can go down 6 feet or more. These deep roots make the grasses resistant to drought, because they reach water that other plants cannot. They also make them resistant to fire. A fire burns the dry leaves, but the roots survive, and new green leaves appear within weeks. Fire, together with the grazing of millions of buffalo, kept trees from taking over.

In the northern plains, the last glaciers left thousands of small hollows in the ground. Seen from the air, many of these ponds are round or oval, like a field of oval mirrors. Each spring they fill with water, and so many ducks nest beside them that the region is sometimes called the duck factory of North America.

The history of the plains also holds a sober lesson. In the early twentieth century, farmers plowed up millions of acres of grass to plant wheat. When a long drought came, from about 1930 to 1940, no deep roots were left to hold the soil, and the wind lifted it into great black clouds of dust. Those years became known as the Dust Bowl, and they taught a sober truth: the grass had been protecting the soil all along.

Today, only a token amount of the original tallgrass prairie survives, less than 4 percent. Even so, scientists study these places to learn how the old grasses hold soil, and some farmers are planting them again.

Questions:
How tall could the tallgrass become?
It reached a person's thigh, then a person's elbow.
How high did the shortgrass grow?
It grew only a few inches high, low enough for a crow to see over it.
Why are the prairie grasses resistant to drought and fire?
Their deep roots reach water that other plants cannot, and the roots survive when fire burns the leaves.
What sober lesson did the Dust Bowl teach?
It taught that the grass had been protecting the soil all along.
How much of the original tallgrass prairie survives today?
Only a token amount survives, less than 4 percent.

lessons.title: Why a Geyser Erupts
lessons.summary: An explanation of how the geysers of Yellowstone work, and how to watch them safely.
lessons.text:
Yellowstone National Park contains about half of all the geysers on Earth. A geyser is a hot spring that, from time to time, throws a fountain of boiling water and steam into the air.

A few miles below the surface lies a huge body of hot, partly melted rock, the engine of everything that happens above it. Rain and melted snow sink through cracks in the rock and are heated deep underground. But a geyser needs more than water and heat. It also needs a narrow underground pipe that the water cannot easily escape from.

That pipe is often sealed by a mineral that the water itself carries. Hot water takes up silica, a hard material made of silicon and oxygen, from the rock around it. Silicon is the same element found in sand, glass and computer chips. As the water cools near the surface, the silica comes out of it and coats the walls of the pipe, sealing it like the inside of a bottle.

Now the process can begin. At the surface, water boils at about 199 degrees Fahrenheit, because the park lies so high above the sea. Deep in the pipe, however, the weight of the water above raises the pressure, and under pressure, water can attain much higher temperatures without boiling. When the water near the top finally boils, some of it spills out. This lowers the pressure below, and the very hot water deep in the pipe turns into steam almost at once. The steam pushes everything above it out of the ground, in a fountain that can attain a height of 100 feet or more.

The most famous geyser in the park, Old Faithful, is known for its consistency. It goes off roughly every 60 to 110 minutes. Its consistency is not perfect, but rangers can usually predict the next show to within about 10 minutes from the length of the last one. A short show is followed by a short wait, and a long show by a long one.

In the interim, visitors lounge on the benches around it, eat lunch or walk the nearby paths. When the time comes, the area turns into a small circus of cameras, phones and excited children. Then, in the interim before the next show, the circus quietly breaks up.

The hot springs can look like a spa, with their blue and orange pools, but they are nothing like a spa. The water is often close to boiling, and some of it is as strong as acid. That is why it is inappropriate, and also dangerous, to leave the paths, to touch the water or to throw coins into the pools. Such inappropriate behavior has injured people and damaged several famous springs.

Questions:
What does a geyser need besides water and heat?
It needs a narrow underground pipe that the water cannot easily escape from.
Why can the water deep in the pipe attain high temperatures without boiling?
The weight of the water above raises the pressure.
How do rangers predict the next show of Old Faithful?
They predict it from the length of the last one.
What do visitors do in the interim between shows?
They lounge on the benches, eat lunch or walk the nearby paths.
Why is it inappropriate to touch the water in the hot springs?
The water is often close to boiling, and some of it is as strong as acid.

lessons.title: How Yellowstone Became a Park
lessons.summary: How stories, pictures and two laws turned Yellowstone into the first national park and protected it.
lessons.text:
In the winter of 1807, a hunter named John Colter, who had traveled west with Lewis and Clark, walked alone through the mountains of what is now Wyoming. He later described a land of boiling springs and hot steam that came out of the ground. Back in the towns of the East, his stories mostly provoked laughter. Few people doubted Colter's courage, but many doubted his honesty.

It took a scientific expedition to change people's minds. In 1871, the government sent a survey to the region, led by Ferdinand Hayden. With him went the photographer William Henry Jackson and the painter Thomas Moran. Hayden's reports described the hot springs in careful detail, but it was the pictures that caused a sensation. Jackson's photographs showed that the strange places were real, and Moran's paintings showed their colors. After this sensation, no one questioned the honesty of the old hunters.

Hayden used this publicity well. He brought the photographs to the Capitol in Washington and showed them to members of Congress. Within a few months, Congress agreed to enact a law that set the land aside "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people." President Ulysses Grant signed the statute on March 1, 1872, and Yellowstone became the first national park in the world.

The new statute, however, had two serious weaknesses. It gave the park almost no money, and it named no punishment for those who broke its rules. Hunters killed animals in the park by the hundreds, and they could not be punished in any real way. Even when they were caught, the most the park could do was to send them away.

By 1886, the situation was so bad that the United States Army was sent to protect the park. Soldiers patrolled the park, but the law was still weak. Then, in March 1894, soldiers caught a man who had been killing some of the last wild buffalo in the country. A writer for a sports magazine happened to be in the park at the time, and his reports about the case created new publicity across the nation. Readers were angry that a man could kill such rare animals and not be punished.

This time, Congress acted quickly. In May 1894, it met at the Capitol to enact a new law that made hunting in the park a crime. From then on, the government could prosecute anyone who hunted there, and the courts could send them to prison or make them pay large fines. For the first time, people who harmed the park's animals could be properly prosecuted.

The history of Yellowstone shows that a park needs more than beautiful land. It needed honest witnesses, pictures that could cause a sensation, publicity that reached the Capitol and, finally, a statute with real force.

Questions:
Why did John Colter's stories mostly provoke laughter?
Many people doubted his honesty.
What caused a sensation after the survey of 1871?
The photographs of William Henry Jackson and the paintings of Thomas Moran caused a sensation.
Where did Hayden show the photographs?
He showed them to members of Congress at the Capitol in Washington.
What were the two weaknesses of the statute of 1872?
It gave the park almost no money, and it named no punishment for those who broke its rules.
What did the law of 1894 allow the government to do?
It allowed the government to prosecute anyone who hunted in the park.

lessons.title: The Redwood Forests
lessons.summary: How the tallest trees on Earth live, grow and survive along the coast of northern California.
lessons.text:
Along the coast of northern California and southern Oregon grows a narrow belt of forest, about 450 miles long and rarely more than 40 miles wide. This is the home of the coast redwood, the tallest tree on Earth. The tallest one known today stands about 380 feet high, and some of these trees have lived for more than 2,000 years.

Many visitors say that walking into an old grove feels like walking into a cathedral. The trunks rise like great columns, the light comes down gently from far above, and people begin to speak in low voices. Even visitors who lead entirely secular lives describe the feeling in religious words. A grove of redwoods is, in a sense, a secular cathedral: a place of silence and wonder that belongs to no single faith.

The forest owes its existence to the sea. In summer the coast receives almost no rain, but cool fog moves in from the ocean on most nights. The tall trees catch the fog in their needles, where it gathers into drops that fall to the ground like rain. Scientists have found that fog is a major contributor of water to these forests; in some groves, it supplies as much as a third of the water the trees use in summer.

The trees are also hard to kill. Their bark can be a foot thick and contains chemicals that protect it from insects and fire. Many old trees carry deep black hollows from fires centuries ago, yet they are still alive. With their broken tops and burned trunks, they are not models of perfection, but their very lack of perfection shows how much they have survived.

Ecologists use the word recruitment for the process by which young plants survive to join a forest. Redwoods produce tiny seeds, but few of them grow into trees, so much of their recruitment comes from the roots instead. When an old tree is cut or damaged, young trees often grow from its roots in a ring around it. Even a fallen giant is not a tomb. As the log slowly breaks down over hundreds of years, plants, insects and young trees live on it.

Since about 1850, logging has removed around 95 percent of the original old forest. What remains survives largely because of civic action. In 1918, a group of citizens founded a society to buy groves and protect them, and civic groups across the state raised money for the cause. Today, park fire crews work like a fire brigade through the dry months, and a brigade may even start small, careful fires to clear the ground, because these forests have always lived with fire. Few landscapes in the country are held in higher esteem, and that esteem has helped to save them.

Questions:
Why do many people call a redwood grove a secular cathedral?
It is a place of silence and wonder that belongs to no single faith.
Why is fog such an important contributor of water?
In summer the coast gets almost no rain, and fog can supply as much as a third of the water the trees use.
How does much of the recruitment of new redwoods happen?
Young trees grow from the roots of old trees, often in a ring around them.
Why is a fallen redwood not a tomb?
As it slowly breaks down, plants, insects and young trees live on it.
How have the remaining forests survived?
They have survived largely because of civic action.

lessons.title: Notes from the Mississippi Delta
lessons.summary: A newspaper correspondent reports on the river's freight, its mud and the land that is disappearing.
lessons.text:
I have worked as a correspondent in many places, but no assignment has taught me as much as my month in the Mississippi delta, at the southern end of Louisiana. Here I found two stories: a river that is a highway for freight, and a land that is slowly sinking into the sea.

The first story begins on the water. Standing on a wooden pier south of New Orleans, I watched a tow move past. On the river, a tow is a powerful boat together with the barges it pushes, all tied into one long block. This one had about 30 barges carrying grain, coal and chemicals. A barge is slow, but it is an efficient way to move freight: with a single gallon of fuel, a barge can move a ton of freight more than 600 miles, far farther than a truck. At the mouth of the river, large ocean ships queue in the Gulf of Mexico. Each one waits in the queue for a river pilot, a local expert who knows the river's moving sand and guides the ship upstream.

The second story is about mud. The Mississippi drains water from more than 30 states and carries millions of gallons to the sea every second. With the water comes mud. For thousands of years, the river dropped this mud near its mouth and slowly built the delta. The new land sank a little under its own weight, but each spring flood brought fresh mud to replace what was lost.

Then people stepped in. After a terrible flood in 1927, the government built high walls of earth, called levees, along the river to protect the towns. The walls worked, but they also kept the mud inside the river, which now carries it straight out into the deep water of the Gulf. Canals dug for shipping and oil let salt water into the marshes, killing the plants that hold them together. Since 1932, Louisiana has lost about 2,000 square miles of land.

The walls are expensive to keep up, and local districts levy taxes on property to pay for them. In Louisiana, counties are called parishes, and a parish councilor I met at a boat ramp explained the difficulty. "We levy taxes to keep the river in," the councilor said, "but the land needs the river to come out."

The state's answer is to work with the river instead of against it. Engineers have cut openings in some walls to inject river water back into the marshes, and they are planning larger projects to inject both water and mud. Scientists hope that this will let the river build land again, as it did for thousands of years.

Questions:
What did the correspondent see from the pier?
From the pier, the correspondent saw a tow: a powerful boat pushing about 30 barges.
Why do ocean ships wait in a queue at the mouth of the river?
Each ship must wait for a river pilot who will guide it upstream.
How did the walls along the river change the delta?
They kept the mud inside the river, so it no longer built new land.
What did the councilor say at the boat ramp?
The councilor said that they levy taxes to keep the river in, but the land needs the river to come out.
Why do engineers inject river water into the marshes?
They hope the water and mud will let the river build land again.

lessons.title: A Summer Diary from the Tundra
lessons.summary: A researcher's diary from a field station in northern Alaska, about frozen ground, the midnight sun and a snowy owl.
lessons.text:
June 2. I arrived at the field station today, far north of the Arctic Circle in Alaska. The station belongs to a university, and its institutional rules are strict but sensible: sign out before you leave, carry a radio and never walk alone on the tundra. I was given a narrow bed, a metal locker for my gear and a notebook. Every page of the notebook has the same printed header: date, weather, soil temperature. My first entry reads: Weather: cold wind, a slate sky. Soil temperature: 1 degree Celsius.

June 5. I now understand why there are no trees here. Only the top foot or two of the soil thaws each summer. Below that, the ground stays frozen all year, as it has for thousands of years. Roots cannot go down, and water cannot drain away, so the summer land is covered in shallow ponds. The plants grow low: mosses, cotton grass and willows no higher than my ankle.

June 9. The sun has not set since I arrived. At midnight it circles low in the north, and the light turns soft and gold. The mosquitoes never sleep at all, so I wear a thin vest with a net over my head whenever I go out.

June 14. Today I saw a snowy owl. She was sitting on a small hill of earth, her white feathers barred with dark lines, watching the ground. Snowy owls nest here on the open tundra and feed mostly on small animals called lemmings. My colleague, who has studied snowy owls for ten years, told me that owls have extremely acute hearing. The face of an owl works like a dish that collects sound, and its hearing is so acute that it can find an animal moving under the snow. An owl that was deaf would starve here, she said, but this owl was anything but deaf: she turned her head at every small sound in the grass.

June 20. The sky was slate gray all day, and it rained. I sat in the common room in my warm vest and wrote the first part of my quarterly report. The report goes to the institutional committee that pays for our work. In it, I describe our most important finding so far: the frozen ground under the station is warming, and the soil is thawing deeper than it did twenty years ago.

June 28. My last week. I emptied my locker, filed my notes and finished the quarterly report. On my final walk, I saw the owl again, still on her hill, still listening. I wrote her into my notebook under the usual header. Weather: clear. Soil temperature: 4 degrees. Owl: present.

Questions:
What does the printed header on each page of the notebook include?
It includes the date, the weather and the soil temperature.
Why are there no trees on the tundra?
Only the top of the soil thaws in summer, so roots cannot go down and water cannot drain away.
Why does the writer wear a vest with a net?
The writer wears it because the mosquitoes never sleep.
Why do owls have such acute hearing?
The face of an owl works like a dish that collects sound.
What is the most important finding in the quarterly report?
The frozen ground under the station is warming, and the soil is thawing deeper than before.

lessons.title: Learning to Live in the Desert
lessons.summary: A newcomer to Tucson learns how the Sonoran Desert smells after rain, stores water and feeds people.
lessons.text:
When I moved to Tucson, Arizona, for a job at a small startup, I thought the desert would be empty. I was wrong. The Sonoran Desert, which covers parts of Arizona, California and Mexico, is one of the richest deserts in the world, and in my first year there, it taught me three lessons.

The first lesson was about rain. The Sonoran Desert has two rainy seasons, a gentle one in winter and a violent one in summer, when storms build over the mountains in the afternoon. The first time it rained, my neighbor Rosa knocked on my door and told me to step outside. The air was full of a sharp, clean scent, like a mix of wet stone and medicine. "That's the creosote bush," Rosa said. This gray-green bush covers huge areas of the desert, and when rain falls on its leaves, it releases this scent.

The second lesson was about storing water. The tall saguaro, the cactus with raised arms that appears in so many photos of the Southwest, grows only in this desert. Its trunk is folded like a closed umbrella. After a rain, the folds open as the plant fills with water, and a large saguaro can store up to 200 gallons.

The third lesson was about food. In late spring, Rosa showed me how to collect the long, dry pods of the mesquite tree. People in this desert have ground these pods into a sweet flour for thousands of years. We made a batch of flour in her kitchen. Then she mixed it with ordinary flour, water and a spoon of honey to make a soft dough, shaped the dough into small flat cakes and cooked them in a dry pan. By the end of the summer, I could make a batch on my own, though I still asked Rosa how many spoons of honey to add.

My own work turned out to be about water, too. The startup I joined builds cheap sensors that tell farmers and gardeners exactly how wet their soil is, so that they use less water. Our founder calls herself a hacker, in the old and friendly sense of the word: a person who loves taking things apart to see how they work. She once explained to me that even electricity here depends on careful water use. About 50 miles west of Phoenix stands the largest power plant in the country, with 3 nuclear reactors. It is far from any lake or large river, so each reactor is cooled with water that has already been used in nearby cities and then cleaned. "That's what a desert does," she said. "It makes you use everything twice." Spoken like a true hacker, I thought.

Questions:
Why did the writer move to Tucson?
The writer moved there for a job at a small startup.
What causes the scent in the air after rain?
The creosote bush releases the scent when rain falls on its leaves.
How did Rosa make the dough?
She mixed mesquite flour with ordinary flour, water and a spoon of honey.
What does the startup build?
It builds cheap sensors that tell farmers and gardeners how wet their soil is.
How is each reactor near Phoenix cooled?
Each reactor is cooled with water that has already been used in nearby cities and then cleaned.

lessons.title: A Ranger at the Rim
lessons.summary: An interview with a park ranger about her work at the Grand Canyon and why the canyon moves people.
lessons.text:
Elena Ruiz has worked as a park ranger at the Grand Canyon for twelve years. We spoke on a bench near the old train depot, a short walk from the edge of the canyon.

How did you first come to the canyon?

By train, like many visitors a hundred years ago. Trains have carried visitors here since 1901, and the depot behind us was built of logs in 1910. I stepped off at this depot when I was 19, looked over the edge and decided that I wanted to work here.

What did becoming a ranger involve?

Training, mostly. And like every federal employee, I took an oath. It's a short oath, but I took it seriously. We also help children become Junior Rangers, and they make a promise to protect the parks. Some of them take that promise more seriously than adults take their oath.

What do visitors ask you most often?

Where the bathrooms are! After that, how the canyon formed. And many people ask where they can buy something to take home. The shops here sell a lot of merchandise: shirts, books, cups. I don't mind the merchandise. If a book about rocks starts a child's interest in science, I'm happy.

Do people react to the canyon in a particular way?

Very often they go quiet. A psychologist who studied visitors here once explained to me what she called awe: the feeling we have when we meet something so large that we cannot fully understand it. According to the psychologist, awe makes people feel small, but in a good way. She found that after a moment of awe, people often show more kindness to strangers. I see that kindness every day. People who were pushing in the parking lot an hour earlier kindly offer each other the best place at the edge.

Does music play a role in how people experience the canyon?

For some people, yes. In 1931, the composer Ferde Grofé wrote a famous piece of music about the canyon, with parts called "Sunrise," "Sunset" and "Cloudburst." The composer tried to show the canyon through sound, and some visitors listen to it on their phones at sunset. A few people come at dawn for a kind of meditation. They sit very still and simply watch the light move down the walls. For them, the meditation is the whole visit.

One commentator recently wrote that the parks have become too crowded. What do you think?

That commentator has a point. But I also understand why people come. Many visitors develop a real attachment to this place, and an attachment like that makes people want to protect it.

What do you say to visitors before they leave?

I thank them kindly and ask them to come back. And I tell them that the canyon is still changing, a little every year.

Questions:
How did Elena Ruiz first come to the canyon?
She came by train and stepped off at the old depot when she was 19.
What did she do when she became a ranger?
Like every federal employee, she took an oath.
What did the psychologist find about awe?
She found that after a moment of awe, people often show more kindness to strangers.
Why does Elena think the visitors' attachment to the canyon is important?
An attachment like that makes people want to protect the place.
